title: Big 12 withdraws lawsuit against Texas Tech filed during Brendan Sorsby saga
content:
The Big 12 Conference has withdrawn its lawsuit against Texas Tech University, school officials and Texas attorney general Ken Paxton, according to court documents obtained Monday by The Athletic. The case, which was related to quarterback Brendan Sorsby’s gambling saga, was voluntarily dismissed with prejudice, meaning it cannot be brought again.

The federal lawsuit was originally filed in U.S. district court in Texas in June, shortly after Sorsby was granted eligibility by a state court ruling in Lubbock County. Sorsby had previously been ruled permanently ineligible by the NCAA for excessive gambling violations.

The Big 12’s lawsuit also came on the heels of a letter from Paxton’s office that warned against any Big 12 penalties against Texas Tech for rostering and playing Sorsby in 2026. (Under state law, the Texas attorney general represents Texas Tech in court.)

The Big 12 argued that Paxton and Texas Tech were violating the league’s First Amendment rights by threatening penalties if the Big 12 enforced its bylaws and sanctions against member schools.

The case never progressed in court, but filing it proved to be a shrewd move by the conference. By filing in federal court on First Amendment grounds — and using the Paxton letter to bolster its argument — the Big 12 put a time crunch on Sorsby, who had to decide between staying at Texas Tech and continuing to fight for his eligibility in court, or applying for the NFL supplemental draft by its summer deadline in hopes of playing in the NFL in 2026.

Facing potential penalties, including a conference championship game ban, neither Texas Tech nor Sorsby wanted to put the program at risk. Sorsby ultimately left the Red Raiders, withdrew his own state lawsuit against the NCAA and accepted his permanent ineligibility ruling in June. He was later denied entrance into the NFL’s supplemental draft this summer and is training for the 2027 NFL Draft next spring.

Last week, the SEC made a similar legal argument in a federal lawsuit against LSU regarding the Tigers potentially rostering former professional football players for the 2026 season. LSU elected not to roster any of those players for Week 1 but could add them later.
